design_detail: Single-author narrative review of chronic tolerance to recreational MDMA, covering subjective reports of declining effect, dose escalation across groups of people with different amounts of past use, binge patterns (stacking and boosting), and candidate mechanisms (liver enzymes, neuroadaptation, behavioural tolerance and serotonergic neurotoxicity). No search strategy, databases, dates, selection criteria or appraisal of the cited studies are reported. The review states at the outset that no laboratory study has given a series of MDMA doses to humans, for ethical reasons, so that chronic tolerance cannot be studied in humans under blind, placebo-controlled conditions, and that the human evidence therefore comes from surveys and interviews of people who use ecstasy recreationally.
can_establish: What the survey and interview literature up to 2004 reported about declining subjective efficacy, dose escalation and bingeing among people who use ecstasy, and what mechanisms had been proposed; it is a map of that literature and of its gaps.
cannot_establish: Whether tolerance to MDMA develops, how fast, to which effects, or by what mechanism: every human figure in the review is self-reported by people who used tablets of unknown content, in cross-sectional comparisons of groups with different amounts of past use, with no measurement of dose, no blinding and no prospective follow-up. It also cannot separate tolerance from the other reasons people take more tablets (tablet strength, setting, polydrug use, expectation).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a review. The human studies it summarizes are surveys and interview studies of people who use ecstasy recreationally, recruited through clubs, universities, the internet and a dance magazine's readership, with samples from 52 to about 1151 people.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated; studies appear to have been chosen by the author's knowledge of the field.
sample.demographics: Not applicable; the samples summarized are mostly young adults with roughly equal numbers of men and women, in Australia, the United Kingdom, the United States and continental Europe.
sample.selection_effects: The review's own selection is unsystematic, and about half of the empirical comparisons it rests on come from the author's own research group (Parrott and Lasky 1998; Parrott et al. 2000, 2001, 2002a, 2002b; Fox et al. 2001a, 2001b, 2002; Scholey et al. 2004, whose first author lists the reviewer as second author). The underlying samples are self-selected people willing to report illegal drug use, with the heaviest use reported by those recruited at clubs and raves.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported numbers of tablets, in lifetime occasions, tablets per occasion and maximum tablets per occasion or per week; no biological verification anywhere, and no measurement of the MDMA content of the tablets taken.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported as study conditions of the surveys summarized: typically one tablet or half a tablet on a first occasion, 1.2-2.0 tablets per occasion for regular use, 3.1-3.7 for the most experienced groups, with maxima of 5 to more than 20 tablets in a session in survey subgroups and 20-40 tablets a weekend in three case histories. Most use is oral; the review notes that about 30% of one Australian sample had snorted MDMA and about 16% had injected it.
exposure.polysubstance: Addressed directly: people who use ecstasy are described as using several drugs, with heavier use linked to a wider range of other drugs; the review states that the contribution of polydrug use to tolerance is unclear and that stimulants might foster cross-tolerance. Tablet content is discussed at length, with the proportion containing MDMA rising to about 80-100% by the late 1990s and average content in United Kingdom forensic samples falling from about 102 mg in 1991 to 73 mg in 2001.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable to the dose-escalation data; some of the cognitive studies it cites tested people after a period of abstinence, which is not specified here.

comparison.controls: Within the studies summarized, comparisons are between groups of people with different amounts of past ecstasy use, and in a few studies against people who had never used it.
comparison.matching: Mostly none; the review singles out Verkes et al. (2001) for comparing moderate and heavy groups matched on duration of use and on cannabis, cocaine, amphetamine and alcohol use.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No study cited has a measurement before first use, so the characteristics that lead some people to escalate and others not are unmeasured; the review raises this as an open question.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Varies by study and is usually not controlled; the review treats polydrug use as a limitation it cannot resolve.

outcomes.instruments: Questionnaire and interview measures of self-reported tolerance, tablets per occasion, maximum tablets, bingeing (defined in one study as continuous use without sleep for 48 hours or more), and self-attributed problems; in the animal literature, serotonin syndrome scores, locomotor activity, operant test batteries, self-administration and post-mortem serotonergic markers.
outcomes.validity_norms: Self-report of illegal drug use without biological verification; tolerance is assessed by asking people whether they feel they have become tolerant, which mixes the pharmacological question with expectation and recall.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Chronic tolerance' is operationalized three ways: people saying effects have declined, people taking more tablets per occasion than less experienced people, and people reporting binge patterns. Only the first is a direct report of reduced effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: the review reports the primary studies' statistics (two chi-square tests for the internet-study tables and an analysis of variance for the three-group comparison) without reanalysis.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; none of the human data is blinded, and the review says plainly that blind, placebo-controlled study of chronic tolerance in humans has not been done.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates and no effect sizes. The figures carried forward are group means and percentages from individual surveys: 1.8 tablets per occasion now against 1.2 when starting (430 people using ecstasy regularly, Verheyden et al. 2003a); 1.45 against 1.80 tablets on a Saturday night in novice and regular groups of 15 each (Parrott and Lasky 1998); 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets per occasion and maxima of 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7) across groups defined by lifetime use of 1-99, 100-499 and 500 or more tablets (14, 14 and 11 people; p<0.01 for the maximum, p<0.10 for the usual dose); a normal dose of 1-2 tablets reported by 100% of 109 in the novice group, 84% of 136 in the moderate group and 62% of 37 in the heaviest group, and a maximum of 10 or more tablets in a week by 0%, 9% and 35% (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, p<0.001); 3.1 against 2.0 tablets per occasion in 21 heavy and 21 moderate club-goers; and 58% of 1151 dance-magazine readers reporting tolerance, with about 85-95% of 430 people using it regularly reporting declining effects.
analysis.covariates: None; the review does not reanalyse.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review; no protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The one study whose pattern runs against dose escalation (Fox et al. 2001b, where the longer-using group took slightly fewer tablets per occasion) is reported and discussed, which counts in the review's favour; but no systematic account is given of how many studies were considered and how many are cited, and two of the three mechanism sections rest on animal work selected without criteria.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across surveys, people who have used ecstasy more report taking more tablets per occasion and much larger maxima than people who have used it less, and a large majority of people using it regularly say the drug's wanted effects have declined with repeated use. Those same comparisons also show that problems attributed to ecstasy rise with lifetime use. All of this is self-reported and cross-sectional, and one study found no dose escalation with longer use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review concludes that chronic tolerance to ecstasy in humans is 'a robust empirical phenomenon', that it often develops rapidly, and that serotonergic neurotoxicity is a plausible and partly unique mechanism for it. The first clause goes beyond what cross-sectional self-report can show: people who escalate may differ from those who do not in ways measured nowhere, the tablets themselves vary in content, and the review itself states that the question cannot be studied in humans under controlled conditions. The neurotoxicity mechanism is argued from animal studies and from a correlation between reported use and reported problems, and the review is explicit that it is a hypothesis.

timeline.event: Two 100 mg doses 24 hours apart in a laboratory: the second dose produced slightly larger effects than the first but smaller than its higher plasma concentrations predicted, with pupil, Maddox-wing and prolactin responses unchanged
Fifty mg followed by 100 mg two hours later: blood pressure and temperature rose in line with concentration while heart rate and the wanted subjective effects did not
A 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg prolonged effects by about an hour without raising peak effects, despite 1.5-fold higher peak concentrations

replication.where_it_stands: The within-session part of the question, which this review explicitly sets aside, has since been studied in controlled laboratory conditions by three groups; the chronic question it addresses is still answered only by surveys, and no prospective human study of repeated recreational use has been published that would settle it.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article carries no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Psychology, University of Wales Swansea. A large share of the empirical comparisons the review relies on are the author's own studies, which the review does not flag.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study following people from their first occasions of ecstasy use, with repeated measurement of the dose actually taken (by tablet analysis or hair or plasma measurement), of the subjective response, and of the setting, so that a decline in effect can be separated from changes in tablet content, context and expectation; in the laboratory, a repeated-dosing design at intervals of days to weeks, which has not been done in humans.

domains.note: No databases, dates, search terms or selection criteria are reported; studies appear to have been chosen by the author's familiarity with the literature.

No formal appraisal. Survey percentages and group means are carried forward without discussion of response rates, recruitment or recall, and a case report of one person's use is quoted at length alongside survey data.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Most of the dose-escalation comparisons (Parrott and Lasky 1998; Fox et al. 2001a, 2001b; Parrott et al. 2000, 2001, 2002a, 2002b; Scholey et al. 2004) are the author's own work, and the review does not say so.

The neurotoxicity mechanism is repeatedly labelled as a hypothesis and the limitations section is candid about polydrug use and unknown tablet content; but the overview states that chronic tolerance is a robust empirical phenomenon without restating that every human datum is self-reported.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against tolerance to MDMA
domains.note: Alternative explanations for taking more tablets (falling tablet strength is examined and set aside; changing setting, expectation, polydrug use and self-selection are not) receive much less space than the tolerance account, and the animal studies that found sensitization rather than tolerance are given a paragraph against several pages for tolerance.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used. The review is valuable as a map: it is explicit that controlled human study of chronic tolerance does not exist, it collects the survey figures in one place, and it reports the one study whose pattern runs the other way. Its selection is unsystematic, it leans heavily on the author's own studies without saying so, and the balance between the tolerance account and its alternatives is uneven. It should be cited for the existence and content of the survey literature, for the dose figures as reported by those surveys, and for the statement that no controlled human study of repeated MDMA dosing over days existed in 2005; claims about tolerance itself should cite the primary studies, and any claim resting only on this review stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3).

key_findings.finding: The review states that there are no laboratory studies giving a series of MDMA doses to humans, because of concerns about serotonergic neurotoxicity, and that it is therefore not possible to investigate chronic tolerance to MDMA in humans under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions; all human evidence in the review comes from studies of people who use ecstasy recreationally.
key_findings.locator: The paragraph beginning 'The pharmacodynamic effects of single doses of MDMA' and the one following it (left column)

key_findings.finding: Self-reported tolerance is common in surveys: 58% of 1151 readers of a dance magazine reported tolerance to ecstasy, and among 430 people who had been using it for about four years, around 85-95% reported a decline in subjective efficacy, described by the authors of that study as the most frequently reported long-term effect. An earlier survey found that 67% of people who had taken it on six or more occasions said positive effects decreased and negative effects increased with successive doses.
key_findings.locator: Subjective reports of tolerance and diminishing responsiveness to MDMA, 2nd-3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Reported dose rises with past use. In 430 people using ecstasy regularly, current use averaged 1.8 tablets a session against 1.2 when they began; across three groups defined by lifetime use (1-99, 100-499 and 500 or more tablets; 14, 14 and 11 people) the usual dose was 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets and the maximum ever taken 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7), with the maximum differing significantly (p<0.01) and the usual dose only at p<0.10.
key_findings.locator: Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 74); Table 1 (p. 74)
key_findings.note: The text gives the highest group's usual dose as 3.7 tablets and its maximum as 10.7, while Table 1 prints 3.7 (SD 3.8) and 10.9 (SD 8.7); the table values are used here.

key_findings.finding: In an internet study of 282 people, a normal dose of 1-2 tablets was reported by 100% of 109 in the novice group (1-9 lifetime occasions), 84% of 136 moderate (10-99) and 62% of 37 in the heaviest group (100 or more), while a maximum of 10 or more tablets in one week was reported by 0%, 9% and 35% of the three groups (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, both p<0.001). In the same sample, self-attributed problems rose with lifetime use: depression 33%, 54% and 65%; memory problems 19%, 52% and 73%; weight loss 10%, 37% and 48%.

One study runs against the escalation pattern: two groups differing mainly in how long they had used ecstasy (3.9 against 10.9 years) and in lifetime consumption (223 against 811 tablets) reported similar doses per occasion, with the longer-using group taking slightly fewer (2.1 against 2.5 tablets, not significant). The review draws from this that long-term use is not invariably linked to dose escalation.
key_findings.locator: Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Binge patterns are described from survey work: taking several tablets at once ('stacking') and repeated tablets over an evening or successive days ('boosting'), with 76% of people using more than weekly having binged at least once against 16% of those using less than monthly; by a stricter definition (continuous use without sleep for 48 hours or more) about a third of 329 people using ecstasy regularly had binged in the previous six months, and those who had reported more physical and psychological side-effects and more days of recent use.

The review reports that falling tablet strength does not explain rising tablet counts: in United Kingdom forensic samples the average MDMA content per tablet was about 102, 90, 103, 99, 100 and 88 mg from 1991 to 1996 and 75, 77, 82, 74 and 73 mg from 1997 to 2001, a fall of about 20% across the mid-1990s with stable values before and after, and two other national surveys found variation without a systematic trend.
key_findings.locator: The paragraph beginning 'A related problem is the issue of dosage' (right column)

key_findings.finding: On mechanisms, the review reports a specialist's view that MDMA's main metabolizing enzyme is not inducible and is largely inactivated by a single dose, so that any tolerance must be pharmacodynamic rather than pharmacokinetic, and that no repeated-dose study of liver enzymes had been done; the animal literature is mixed, with some studies showing tolerance to behavioural and serotonin-syndrome measures and two showing the opposite (sensitization).
key_findings.locator: Animal data on putative underlying mechanisms, 1st paragraph (p. 76) and the paragraphs on behavioural measures (pp. 76-77)
key_findings.note: The enzyme statement is a personal communication quoted in the review, not a published result.

key_findings.finding: The review proposes that serotonergic axon-terminal loss may itself cause the loss of effect, so that reduced efficacy, dose escalation and rising problems develop together, and states that this is an additional possible factor rather than an alternative to the usual mechanisms; it also notes that intermittent use in cool, quiet settings may limit how fast tolerance develops.
key_findings.locator: Serotonergic neurotoxicity and chronic tolerance to MDMA, last two paragraphs (p. 78); Overview, last paragraph (p. 80)

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the most experienced group's average maximum as 10.7 tablets per occasion while Table 1 on the same page prints 10.9 (SD 8.7); the usual dose is 3.7 in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small discrepancy in a figure that is quoted widely; the table value should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 reports the lifetime-use groups as 'Low 1-99, Medium 100-499, High 500+' tablets with 14, 14 and 11 people and a two-tailed significance of p<0.10 for the usual dose, yet the running text describes the usual-dose difference without that qualification.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose-per-occasion difference across lifetime-use groups in that study did not reach conventional significance; only the maximum did.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 2 and 3 describe the same internet study and the same participants: Table 2 gives group sizes of 109, 136 and 37, which sum to the 282 people the text near Table 3 reports, and Table 3's legend states that it is the same study and participants as Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Consistent, but the reader should note that the dose figures and the problem figures come from one sample, so the correlation between heavier use and more problems within that sample is not independent evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: A large share of the empirical comparisons are the author's own studies, and the review nowhere states this.
reporting_issues.consequence: The convergence of the cited findings is weaker than it appears, because the studies share investigators, recruitment routes and measures (METHODS 6.3, overlapping evidence).

reporting_issues.issue: A statement central to the mechanism argument, that MDMA's main metabolizing enzyme cannot be induced and is inactivated by a single dose, is sourced to a personal communication from 2002 and includes a dosing recommendation in the quoted text.
reporting_issues.consequence: An unpublished opinion is doing load-bearing work in the mechanism section; it cannot be checked, and the dosing sentence inside it must not be carried into the encyclopedia.

reporting_issues.issue: Case histories of three people using 20-40 tablets a weekend, including one injecting large amounts, are presented beside survey percentages without a change of register.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take extreme case reports as representative; they are selected cases from a clinic, and the review's own surveys put the common pattern at one to three tablets.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 71-83 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2005_ChronicToleranceReview.pdf), full text including Tables 1-3; reference list read for the authorship of the cited studies.
